title: Articles (a, an, the)
shortDescription: The smallest words in English carry the biggest number of exam traps — sound-based rules, zero article, and the exceptions everyone forgets.
genZNote: Three tiny words, endless ways to get them wrong. Master this and you've defused one of the exam's favourite landmines.

sections.heading: Indefinite vs definite articles
sections.body: 'A' and 'an' are indefinite articles — used with a singular countable noun when it is not specific or is being mentioned for the first time ('I saw A dog'). 'The' is the definite article — used when the noun is specific, already known, or unique ('THE dog I saw yesterday'; 'THE sun'). Plural and uncountable nouns generally take no article when speaking in general ('Dogs are loyal', not 'The dogs are loyal', unless referring to specific dogs).

sections.heading: a vs an — it's about SOUND, not spelling
bullets: Use 'an' before a word that begins with a VOWEL SOUND, not necessarily a vowel letter: an hour (silent h), an MBA (sounds like 'em'), an honest man.
Use 'a' before a word that begins with a CONSONANT SOUND, even if the letter is a vowel: a university (sounds like 'yoo'), a European trip (sounds like 'yuro'), a one-rupee coin (sounds like 'won').
This 'sound, not spelling' rule is one of the most repeated exam traps — always sound the word out before choosing a/an.

sections.heading: When to use 'the'
bullets: Something unique in the world/context: the sun, the Prime Minister, the Constitution.
Superlatives and ordinal numbers: the best, the first, the tallest.
Rivers, oceans, seas, mountain ranges, groups of islands, deserts: the Ganga, the Himalayas, the Sahara — but NOT single mountains or lakes (Everest, Lake Victoria — no article).
Names of countries that are unions/plurals/have 'of' in them: the United States, the United Kingdom, the Republic of India — but NOT single-word country names (India, France).
Musical instruments: play THE guitar (but play chess/cricket — games take no article).

sections.heading: Zero article (no article at all)
bullets: General/plural or uncountable nouns speaking generally: 'Milk is nutritious', 'Books are our friends.'
Most proper nouns: names of people, cities, single countries, single mountains/lakes: Mumbai, India, Everest.
Names of languages and most academic subjects: 'She speaks French', 'He studies Physics.'
Meals, means of transport with 'by': breakfast, lunch; by bus, by train (but 'in THE bus' when referring to a specific bus).
Abstract nouns used generally: 'Honesty is the best policy' (no article before Honesty).

sections.heading: Frequently tested exceptions
sections.body: 'Go to school/college/church/bed/prison' takes no article when referring to the general PURPOSE of the place (studying, worship, sleeping, being an inmate); 'go to THE school' means physically going to the building for some other reason (e.g. to vote). Similarly, 'in hospital' (as a patient, British usage) vs 'in THE hospital' (visiting, or American usage) — Indian competitive exams generally follow the 'no article for purpose' pattern.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Articles (a, an, the) mark whether a noun is non-specific (a/an), specific (the), or general with no article at all — decided mainly by sound and context, not spelling.
keyFacts: 'A/an' is chosen by the SOUND that follows, not the letter — an hour, a university.
Rivers, mountain ranges, and multi-word/union country names take 'the'; single mountains and single-word country names don't.
General statements with plural or uncountable nouns take no article.
commonConfusion: 'The Everest' and 'an university' are both classic wrong forms students write from habit.

highYieldFacts: 'An hour', 'an honest man', 'an MBA' — all use 'an' due to a vowel SOUND despite consonant spelling in two of them.
'A European', 'a university', 'a one-eyed man' all use 'a' due to a consonant SOUND despite a vowel letter.
commonTraps: Choosing a/an by looking only at the spelling of the next word instead of its sound.
Adding 'the' before a single-word country name or single mountain (the India, the Everest).
Forgetting 'the' before superlatives and ordinal numbers.
mustRemember: Say the next word out loud in your head — vowel sound needs 'an', consonant sound needs 'a', regardless of spelling.
possibleQuestions: Fill in the blank: 'She is ___ honest and ___ hardworking student.' (an, a)
Spot the error: 'He is going to school to attend the parents' meeting.' (needs THE school — it's not for the purpose of studying)
